tweets: In 1565, an entire capital city was reduced to rubble — palaces, markets, elephant stables, all abandoned overnight. One temple in the ruins never stopped ringing its bells.

This is the Virupaksha Temple at Hampi, Karnataka — dedicated to Shiva as Virupaksha, alongside the goddess Pampa (namesake of the river and the town). A shrine has stood here since at least the 7th century, per early Chalukya-era inscriptions.

For centuries it stayed a modest riverside shrine. Then Vijayanagara made Hampi its capital, and its kings poured wealth in — culminating in emperor Krishnadevaraya's soaring 50m gopuram, raised in 1510 to mark his own coronation.

Vijayanagara's builders even hid a quiet trick inside: a small opening that projects an inverted image of that giant gopuram onto an inner wall — a working pinhole camera obscura, centuries before the term existed.

In 1565 the empire fell and the city around it was left to ruin. But Virupaksha's priests never broke the daily rituals — 1,300+ years on, they still light the lamps at this UNESCO World Heritage site. Follow @yddoseOfHistory for your daily dose of history 🛕
